entries.d3a5b4fb0cc740647520830273a1fcfd09ff642e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8100"/><div sID="gen12605" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8100"/>15. An objection entertained by Solomon<div eID="gen12605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the days of his vanity--</hi>his apostasy (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ec 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">Job 21:7</reference>).<div eID="gen12606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">just ... perisheth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.13">1Ki 21:13</reference>). Temporal not eternal death (<reference osisRef="John.10.28">Joh 10:28</reference>). But see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>; "just" is probably a self-justiciary.<div eID="gen12607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wicked ... prolongeth--</hi>See the antidote to the abuse of this statement in <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">Ec 8:12</reference>. <div eID="gen12608" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab157ef05a605d5dab0634cc2d9fb536457b016a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8101"/><div sID="gen12609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8101"/>16. Holden makes <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference> the scoffing inference of the objector, and <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.17">Ec 7:17</reference> the answer of Solomon, now repentant. So (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">1Co 15:32</reference>) the skeptic's objection; (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.33">1Co 15:33</reference>) the answer. However, "Be not righteous over much," may be taken as Solomon's words, forbidding a self-made righteousness of outward performances, which would wrest salvation from God, instead of receiving it as the gift of His grace. It is a fanatical, pharisaical righteousness, separated from God; for the "fear of God" is in antithesis to it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ec 7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.3">5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.1-Matt.7.9">Mt 6:1-7; 9</reference>:14; 23:23, 24; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Ro 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen12609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">over wise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.3">Ro 12:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.16">16</reference>), presumptuously self-sufficient, as if acquainted with the whole of divine truth.<div eID="gen12610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destroy thyself--</hi>expose thyself to needless persecution, austerities and the wrath of God; hence to an untimely death. "Destroy thyself" answers to "perisheth" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>); "righteous over much," to "a just man." Therefore in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference> it is self-justiciary, not a truly righteous man, that is meant. <div eID="gen12611" type="x-p"/>
entries.431492b07fd291ee1f2a0146b819c66e04826196: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8102"/><div sID="gen12612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8102"/><hi type="bold">17. over much wicked--</hi>so worded, to answer to "righteous over much." For if not taken thus, it would seem to imply that we may be wicked a little. "Wicked" refers to "wicked man" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>); "die before thy time," to "prolongeth his life," antithetically. There may be a wicked man spared to "live long," owing to his avoiding gross excesses (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>). Solomon says, therefore, Be not so foolish (answering antithetically to "over wise," <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>), as to run to such excess of riot, that God will be provoked to cut off prematurely thy day of grace (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.5">Ro 2:5</reference>). The precept is addressed to a sinner. Beware of aggravating thy sin, so as to make thy case desperate. It refers to the days of Solomon's "vanity" (apostasy, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>), when only such a precept would be applicable. By litotes it includes, "Be not wicked at all." <div eID="gen12612" type="x-p"/>
entries.8479c528a318da454652887aa25d8e11c253024a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8103"/><div sID="gen12613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8103"/><hi type="bold">18. this ... this--</hi>the two opposite excesses (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.17">17</reference>), fanatical, self-wise righteousness, and presumptuous, foolhardy wickedness.<div eID="gen12613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that feareth God shall come forth of them all--</hi>shall escape all such extremes (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.7">Pr 3:7</reference>). <div eID="gen12614" type="x-p"/>
entries.e56d2eecb5c5116d7c8b8e2c49a0c2b0aa4e30b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8104"/><div sID="gen12615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8104"/>19. Hebrew, "The wisdom," that is, the true wisdom, religion (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen12615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">than ten mighty--</hi>that is, able and valiant generals (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.12">Ec 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.13-Eccl.9.18">9:13-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.22">Pr 21:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.5">24:5</reference>). These "watchmen wake in vain, except the Lord keep the city" (<reference osisRef="Ps.127.1">Psa 127:1</reference>). <div eID="gen12616" type="x-p"/>
entries.17505173adf8ad6805b245ceebd913d51cbe7eb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8105"/><div sID="gen12617" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8105"/>20. Referring to <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>. Be not "self-righteous," seek not to make thyself "just" before God by a superabundance of self-imposed performances; "for true 'wisdom,' or 'righteousness,' shows that there is not a just man," &c. <div eID="gen12617" type="x-p"/>
entries.e03d2bfe5a971980790c9f25c19e959227dc9f9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8106"/><div sID="gen12618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8106"/>21. As therefore thou being far from perfectly "just" thyself, hast much to be forgiven by God, do not take too strict account, as the self-righteous do (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.9">Lu 18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">11</reference>), and thereby shorten their lives (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">16</reference>), of words spoken against thee by others, for example, thy servant: Thou art their "fellow servant" before God (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.32-Matt.18.35">Mt 18:32-35</reference>). <div eID="gen12618" type="x-p"/>
entries.7826abf230e90465d968fe96236d1f9e92544465: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8107"/><div sID="gen12619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8107"/>22. (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.44">1Ki 2:44</reference>). <div eID="gen12619" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9ea2b518def0a24918e80a9ec3087d95982c315: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8108"/><div sID="gen12620" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8108"/><hi type="bold">23. All this--</hi>resuming the "all" in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15-Eccl.7.22">Ec 7:15-22</reference> is therefore the fruit of his dearly bought experience in the days of his "vanity."<div eID="gen12620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will be wise--</hi>I tried to "be wise," independently of God. But true wisdom was then "far from him," in spite of his human wisdom, which he retained by God's gift. So "over wise" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>). <div eID="gen12621" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b850de5236b69ae32c357e2ac050eac673a2c45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8109"/><div sID="gen12622" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8109"/><hi type="bold">24. That ... far off ... deep--</hi>True wisdom is so when sought independently of "fear of God" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ec 7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.30.12">De 30:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.7">Job 11:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.11.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.28.12-Job.28.20">28:12-20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">Psa 64:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.6">Ro 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.7">7</reference>). <div eID="gen12622" type="x-p"/>
entries.f35b3354785f31129632d0252c316efac22f5fcb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8110"/><div sID="gen12623" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8110"/>25. Literally, "I turned myself and mine heart to." A phrase peculiar to Ecclesiastes, and appropriate to the penitent turning back to commune with his heart on his past life.<div eID="gen12623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wickedness of folly--</hi>He is now a step further on the path of penitence than in <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">Ec 1:17</reference>; 2:12, where "folly" is put without "wickedness" prefixed.<div eID="gen12624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reason--</hi>rather, "the right estimation" of things. Holden translates also "foolishness (that is, sinful folly, answering to 'wickedness' in the parallel) of madness" (that is, of man's mad pursuits). <div eID="gen12625" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cd4da61006260d859643a32626576fdccdb5f1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8111"/><div sID="gen12626" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8111"/>26. "I find" that, of all my sinful follies, none has been so ruinous a snare in seducing me from God as idolatrous women (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.3">1Ki 11:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.3">Pr 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.14">22:14</reference>). As "God's favor is better than life," she who seduces from God is "more bitter than death."<div eID="gen12626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whoso pleaseth God--</hi>as Joseph (<reference osisRef="Gen.39.2">Ge 39:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.9">3, 9</reference>). It is God's grace alone that keeps any from falling. <div eID="gen12627" type="x-p"/>
entries.42e913d7f1e7ea8bf632c5c0fba61e65ef7290d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8112"/><div sID="gen12628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8112"/><hi type="bold">27. this--</hi>namely, what follows in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.28">Ec 7:28</reference>.<div eID="gen12628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counting one by one--</hi>by comparing one thing with another [Holden and Maurer].<div eID="gen12629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">account--</hi>a right estimate. But <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.28">Ec 7:28</reference> more favors Gesenius. "Considering women one by one." <div eID="gen12630" type="x-p"/>
entries.05d2c2c938dc9219a607c14d30059dcfe766b940: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8113"/><div sID="gen12631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8113"/>28. Rather, referring to his past experience, "Which my soul sought further, but I found not."<div eID="gen12631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one man--</hi>that is, worthy of the name, "man," "upright"; not more than one in a thousand of my courtiers (<reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1">Psa 12:1</reference>). Jesus Christ alone of men fully realizes the perfect ideal of "man." "Chiefest among ten thousand" (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>). No perfect "woman" has ever existed, not even the Virgin Mary. Solomon, in the word "thousand," alludes to his three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines. Among these it was not likely that he should find the fidelity which one true wife pays to one husband. Connected with <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ec 7:26</reference>, not an unqualified condemnation of the sex, as <reference osisRef="Prov.12.4">Pr 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.10">31:10</reference>, &c., prove. <div eID="gen12632" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6d21e61b4aab7caa8c723852d15e78883615a73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8114"/><div sID="gen12633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8114"/>29. The "only" way of accounting for the scarcity of even comparatively upright men and women is that, whereas God made man upright, they (men) have, &c. The only account to be "found" of the origin of evil, the great mystery of theology, is that given in Holy Writ (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.1-Gen.3.24">Ge 2:1-3:24</reference>). Among man's "inventions" was the one especially referred to in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ec 7:26</reference>, the bitter fruits of which Solomon experienced, the breaking of God's primeval marriage law, joining one man to "one" woman (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.4">Mt 19:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.6">5, 6</reference>). "Man" is singular, namely, Adam; "they," plural, Adam, Eve, and their posterity. <chapter eID="Eccl.7"/>

entries.2878a8872a23b176399bdacf3a10052d8f8a1211: <div eID="gen25510" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25511" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25512" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25512" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25511" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25513" type="x-p"/> The value of a good name, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.1">Ecc 7:1</reference>. Advantages of sorrow and correction, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.2-Ecc.7.5">Ecc 7:2-5</reference>. The emptiness of a fool's joy, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.6">Ecc 7:6</reference>. Of oppression, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference>. The end better than the beginning, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.8">Ecc 7:8</reference>. Against hastiness of spirit, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.9">Ecc 7:9</reference>. Comparison of former and present times, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.10">Ecc 7:10</reference>. Excellence of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.11">Ecc 7:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.12">Ecc 7:12</reference>. Of the dispensations of Providence, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.13-Ecc.7.15">Ecc 7:13-15</reference>. Against extremes, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.16-Ecc.7.18">Ecc 7:16-18</reference>. The strength of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.19">Ecc 7:19</reference>. Man is ever liable to sin and mistake, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.20">Ecc 7:20</reference>. We should guard our words, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.21">Ecc 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.22">Ecc 7:22</reference>. Difficulty of obtaining wisdom, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.23-Ecc.7.25">Ecc 7:23-25</reference>, A bad woman dangerous, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.26">Ecc 7:26</reference>. There are few who are really upright, <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.27-Ecc.7.29">Ecc 7:27-29</reference>. <div eID="gen25513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25514" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25515" type="x-p"/> A good name - Unsatisfactory as all sublunary things are, yet still there are some which are of great consequence, and among them a good name. The place is well paraphrased in the following verses: "A spotless name, <div eID="gen25515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25516" type="x-p"/> By virtuous deeds acquired, is sweeter far <div eID="gen25516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25517" type="x-p"/> Than fragant balms, whose odors round diffused <div eID="gen25517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25518" type="x-p"/> Regale the invited guests. Well may such men <div eID="gen25518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25519" type="x-p"/> Rejoice at death's approach, and bless the hours <div eID="gen25519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25520" type="x-p"/> That end their toilsome pilgrimage; assured <div eID="gen25520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25521" type="x-p"/> That till the race of life is finish'd none <div eID="gen25521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25522" type="x-p"/> Can be completely blest."
entries.4856cbe49d345a070be0bd0671c455801ed053d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25523" type="x-p"/> It is better to go to the house of mourning - Birthdays were generally kept with great festivity, and to these the wise man most probably refers; but according to his maxim, the miseries of life were so many and so oppressive that the day of a man's death was to be preferred to the day of his birth. But, in dependently of the allusion, it is much more profitable to visit the house of mourning for the dead than the house of festivity. In the former we find occasion for serious and deeply edifying thoughts and reflections; from the latter we seldom return with one profitable thought or one solid impression.
entries.4b623da436d8ca48ef1d792a95aabfb0df0bbfbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25524" type="x-p"/> Sorrow is better than laughter - The reason is immediately given; for by the sorrow of the countenance - the grief of heart that shows itself in the countenance: - <div eID="gen25524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25525" type="x-p"/> The heart is made better - In such cases, most men try themselves at the tribunal of their own consciences, and resolve on amendment of life.
entries.15c4e7328ed9bb80deaf0d8b75c8f1af033cb0cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen25525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25526" type="x-p"/> The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning - A wise man loves those occasions from which he can derive spiritual advantage; and therefore prefers visiting the sick, and sympathizing with those who have suffered privations by death. But the fool - the gay, thoughtless, and giddy - prefers places and times of diversion and amusement. Here he is prevented from seriously considering either himself or his latter end. The grand fault and misfortune of youth.
entries.381f1980950e4917d0a0acdf16cb095039c4e815: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen25526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25527" type="x-p"/> For as the crackling of thorns - They make a great noise, a great blaze; and are extinguished in a few moments. Such indeed, comparatively, are the joys of life; they are noisy, flashy, and transitory.
entries.2974907b8406a56148ea2987001648ec54b88a13: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen25527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25528" type="x-p"/> Oppression maketh a wise man mad - This has been translated with good show of reason, "Surely oppression shall give lustre to a wise man: but a gift corrupteth the heart." <div eID="gen25528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25529" type="x-p"/> The chief difference here is in the word יהולל yeholel, which, from the root הלל halal, signiffes to glister, irradiate, as well as to move briskly, to be mad, furious, in a rage; and certainly the former meaning suits this place best. We cannot think that the wise man - he that is truly religious, (for this is its meaning in the language of Solomon), can be made mad by any kind of oppression; but as he trusts in God, so in patience he possesses his soul.
entries.47fe54c024e788b2099cbe204c259b67b596ea5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25530" type="x-p"/> Better is the end - We can then judge of the whole, and especially if the matter relate to the conduct of Divine Providence. At the beginning we are often apt to make very rash conjectures, and often suppose that such and such things are against us; and that every thing is going wrong. Dr. Byrom gives good advice on such a subject: - "With patient mind thy course of duty run: <div eID="gen25530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25531" type="x-p"/> God nothing does, nor suffers to be done, <div eID="gen25531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25532" type="x-p"/> But thou wouldst do thyself, couldst thou but see <div eID="gen25532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25533" type="x-p"/> The and of all events, as well as He." <div eID="gen25533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25534" type="x-p"/> I may add, in the words of our paraphrast: - "Wait the result, nor ask with frantic rage <div eID="gen25534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25535" type="x-p"/> Why God permits such things. His ways, though now <div eID="gen25535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25536" type="x-p"/> Involved in clouds and darkness, will appear <div eID="gen25536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25537" type="x-p"/> All right, when from thine eyes the mist is cleared. <div eID="gen25537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25538" type="x-p"/> Till then, to learn submission to his will <div eID="gen25538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25539" type="x-p"/> More wisdom shows, than vainly thus to attempt <div eID="gen25539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25540" type="x-p"/> Exploring what thou canst not comprehend, <div eID="gen25540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25541" type="x-p"/> And God for wisest ends thinks fit to hide." <div eID="gen25541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25542" type="x-p"/> C.
entries.7bb694cb6ef65a4f1ffac896e547b88983802b99: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25543" type="x-p"/> Anger resteth in the bosom of fools - A wise man, off his guard, may feel it for a moment: but in him it cannot rest: it is a fire which he immediately casts out of his breast. But the fool - the man who is under the dominion of his own tempers, harbors and fosters it, till it takes the form of malice, and then excites him to seek full revenge on those whom he deems enemies. Hence that class of dangerous and empty fools called duellists.
entries.983328192a5aeb66a230a63d048cd3bb867d68d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen25543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25544" type="x-p"/> The former days were better than these? - This is a common saying; and it is as foolish as it is common. There is no weight nor truth in it; but men use it to excuse their crimes, and the folly of their conduct. "In former times, say they, men might be more religious, use more self-denial, be more exemplary." This is all false. In former days men were wicked as they are now, and religion was unfashionable: God also is the same now as he was then; as just, as merciful, as ready to help: and there is no depravity in the age that will excuse your crimes, your follies, and your carelessness. <div eID="gen25544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25545" type="x-p"/> Among the oriental proverbs I find the following: "Many say, This is a corrupt age. This mode of speaking is not just, it is not the age that is corrupt, but the men of the age."
entries.5a75425d8f02cdfd73b549af9410415eb8e3833f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen25545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25546" type="x-p"/> Wisdom is good with an inheritance - In this chapter Solomon introduces many observations which appear to be made by objectors against his doctrine; and as he was satisfied of their futility, he proposes them in their own full strength, and then combats and destroys them. It is quite necessary to attend to this; else we shall take the objector's words for those of Solomon; and think, as some have done, that the wise man contradicts and refutes himself. Observations, reflections, and objections of friends and adversaries are frequently introduced in the works of ancient authors, without mentioning them as such. This is frequent, more particularly in ethic writers; and we have many specimens in Horace, and without this distinction, it would be impossible to make sense of some of his writings. Here, an objector who had listened to the wise man declaiming in favor of wisdom, suddenly interrupts him, and says in effect, "I grant the truth of what you have said. Wisdom is very good in its place; but what is it without property? A man who has a good inheritance may be profited by wisdom, because it will show him how to manage it to the best advantage."
entries.dbefa5ec6f5f0d8d19d4cc76664e2f30b553b52a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen25546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25547" type="x-p"/> Wisdom is a defense - To whom Solomon answers: All true wisdom is most undoubtedly a great advantage to men in all circumstances; and money is also of great use: but it cannot be compared to wisdom. Knowledge of Divine and human things is a great blessing. Money is the means of supporting our animal life: but wisdom - the religion of the true God - gives life to them that have it. Money cannot procure the favor of God, nor give life to the soul.
entries.c9913a3735c0db2e2577d9d94c37c7b21fc6b9a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen25547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25548" type="x-p"/> Consider the work of God - Such is the nature of his providence, that it puts money into the hands of few: but wisdom is within the reach of all. The first is not necessary to happiness; therefore, it is not offered to men; the latter is; and therefore God, in his goodness, offers it to the whole human race. The former can rarely be acquired, for God puts it out of the reach of most men, and you cannot make that straight which he has made crooked; the latter may be easily attained by every person who carefully and seriously seeks it from God.
entries.261c9dd0fbc65d489a271fd6ee5b78631c823c33: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen25548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25549" type="x-p"/> In the day of prosperity be joyful - When ye receive these temporal gifts from God, enjoy them, and be thankful to the Giver: but remember, this sunshine will not always last. God has balanced prosperity and adversity against each other; and were it not so, how many would put the former in the place of God himself!
entries.4300e6d9e3564f470845d4167907f9dca6376b8f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen25549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25550" type="x-p"/> There is a just man that perisheth - This is another objection as if he had said, "I also have had considerable experience; and I have not discovered any marked approbation of the conduct of the righteous, or disapprobation of that of the wicked. On the contrary, I have seen a righteous man perish, while employed in the work of righteousness; and a wicked man prosperous, and even exalted, while living wickedly. The former is indeed a victim to his righteousness, while the life and prosperity of the latter were preserved: hence I conclude, it is not prudent, whatever good there may be in religion, and whatever excellence in wisdom, that men should be overmuch righteous, or over-wise: for why should they by austerity and hard study destroy themselves?" So far the objector.
entries.2025bfc0cd6224c1654fbbd42462c0b0bd4919c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen25550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25551" type="x-p"/> Why shouldest thou destroy thyself? - תשומם tishshomem, make thyself desolate, so that thou shalt be obliged to stand alone; neither make thyself over-wise, תתחכם tithchaccam, do not pretend to abundance of wisdom. Why shouldest thou be so singular? In other words, and in modern language, "There is no need of all this watching, fasting, praying, self-denial, etc., you carry things to extremes. Why should you wish to be reputed singular and precise?" To this the man of God answers:
entries.707fd3f1f2fc35061939b8e517ada7ea710d4668: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen25551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25552" type="x-p"/> Be not overmuch wicked, neither be thou foolish: why shouldest thou die before thy time? - אל תרשע הרבה al tirsha harbeh. Do not multiply wickedness, do not add direct opposition to godliness to the rest of your crimes. Why should you provoke God to destroy you before your time? Perdition will come soon enough. If you will not turn from your sins, and avoid it finally, yet keep out of it as long as you can. <div eID="gen25552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25553" type="x-p"/> It cannot be supposed, except by those who are totally unacquainted with the nature of true religion, that a man may have too much holiness, too much of the life of God in his soul! And yet a learned doctor, in three sermons on this text, has endeavored to show, out-doing Solomon's infidel, "the sin, folly, and danger of being righteous overmuch." O rare darkness!
entries.908fcf6bd66e1e34885b170c46133f73c1154bab: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen25553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25554" type="x-p"/> It is good that thou shouldest take hold or this - Do not let such an observation slip: take hold of this; do not forget that. Get what you can in an honest way; but do not forget to get true religion; for he that fears God will be saved from all evil.
entries.67404f94716385541a36f0fbac832d41aee491bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen25554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25555" type="x-p"/> Wisdom strengtheneth the wise - One wise, thoroughly learned, and scientific man, may be of more use in fortifying and defending a city, than ten princes. Witness the case of Syracuse, when attacked by the Romans both by sea and land. Archimedes, by his engines, burnt and dashed their fleet to pieces, and destroyed all that came near the walls. And had not the city been betrayed and he killed, all their force and skill could not have taken it.
entries.c24ecd65cca74deff6db6208e985a279e5d18a71: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen25555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25556" type="x-p"/> There is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not - לא יחטא lo yechta, that may not sin. There is not a man upon earth, however just he may be, and habituated to do good, but is peccable - liable to commit sin; and therefore should continually watch and pray, and depend upon the Lord. But the text does not say, the just man does commit sin, but simply that he may sin; and so our translators have rendered it in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.25">1Sam 2:25</reference>, twice in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.31">1Kgs 8:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.46">1Kgs 8:46</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.36">2Chr 6:36</reference>; and the reader is requested to consult the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.46">1Kgs 8:46</reference>, where the proper construction of this word may be found, and the doctrine in question is fully considered.
entries.1c5e873aded372eb38915a8a895650fbf599bef7: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen25556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25557" type="x-p"/> Also take no heed unto all words that are spoken - This is good advice, and much for every man's peace through life. <div eID="gen25557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25558" type="x-p"/> Thy servant curse thee - מקללך mekallelecha, make light of thee, speak evil of thee.
entries.b4aabc6703d8571570a21bd4e2f955dd1086c1b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen25558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25559" type="x-p"/> Thou thyself - hast cursed others - קללת kalalta, thou hast spoken evil; hast vilified others. O, who is free from evil speaking, from uncharitable speaking; from detailing their neighbor's faults, from whispering, talebearing, and backbiting? Do not wonder if God, in his justice, permit thee to be calumniated, seeing thou hast so frequently calumniated others. See my discourse on <reference osisRef="Psa.15.1-Psa.15.5">Psa 15:1-5</reference> (note).
entries.5572ce31d725a6bb402d5e6911536944381ca155: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen25559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25560" type="x-p"/> All this have I proved by wisdom - These rules I have laid down for my own conduct, and sought after more wisdom; but have fallen far short of what I wished to be.
entries.f5d04fe8d5d1dbab980580b88be00542ef277176: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen25560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25561" type="x-p"/> That which is far off - Though the wisdom that is essential to our salvation may be soon learned, through the teaching of the Spirit of wisdom, yet in wisdom itself there are extents and depths which none can reach or fathom.
entries.f1edce9a01c2fa119400641537c7bc37a2c42c8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen25561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25562" type="x-p"/> I applied mine heart - I cast about, סבותי sabbothi, I made a circuit; I circumscribed the ground I was to traverse; and all within my circle I was determined to know, and to investigate, and to seek out wisdom, and the reason of things. Has man reason and understanding? If so, then this is his work. God as much calls him to use these powers in this way, as to believe on the Lord Jesus that he may be saved; and he that does not, according to the means in his power, is a slothful servant, from whom God may justly take away the misemployed or not used talent, and punish him for his neglect. Every doctrine of God is a subject both for reason and faith to work on. <div eID="gen25562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25563" type="x-p"/> To know the wickedness of folly, even of foolishness and madness - "And my own heart, with scrutiny severe, <div eID="gen25563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25564" type="x-p"/> By far the harder task survey'd; intent <div eID="gen25564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25565" type="x-p"/> To trace that wisdom which from heaven descends, <div eID="gen25565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25566" type="x-p"/> Fountain of living waters, and to explore <div eID="gen25566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25567" type="x-p"/> The source of human folly, whose foul streams <div eID="gen25567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25568" type="x-p"/> Intoxicate and kill." - C.
entries.bbc5cd90a5cb6bad4480f3f93e3430304ffc3851: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen25568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25569" type="x-p"/> And I find more bitter than death the woman - After all his investigation of the wickedness of folly, and the foolishness of madness, he found nothing equally dangerous and ruinous with the blandishments of cunning women. When once the affections are entangled, escape without ruin is almost impossible. <div eID="gen25569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25570" type="x-p"/> Whoso pleaseth God - The man who walks with God, and he alone, shall escape this sore evil: and even he that fears God, if he get with an artful woman, may be soon robbed of his strength, and become like other men. A bad or artful woman is represented as a company of hunters, with nets, gins, etc., to catch their prey.
entries.b8fba2dd2a4a4f4d67f846029d97528bddf269c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen25570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25571" type="x-p"/> Counting one by one - I have gone over every particular. I have compared one thing with another; man with woman, his wisdom with her wiles; his strength with her blandishments; his influence with her ascendancy; his powers of reason with her arts and cunning; and in a thousand men, I have found one thoroughly upright man; but among one thousand women I have not found one such. This is a lamentable account of the state of morals in Judea, in the days of the wise King Solomon. Thank God! it would not be difficult to get a tithe of both in the same number in the present day. <div eID="gen25571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25572" type="x-p"/> The Targum gives this a curious turn: "There is another thing which my soul has sought, but could not find: a man perfect and innocent, and without corruption, from the days of Adam until Abraham the just was born; who was found faithful and upright among the thousand kings who came together to construct the tower of Babel: but a woman like to Sarah among the wives of all those kings I have not found."
entries.8d3f254d693960cf1a3e04b655e042811d594d2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen25572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25573" type="x-p"/> Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright - Whatever evil may be now found among men and women, it is not of God; for God made them all upright. This is a singular verse, and has been most variously translated: עשה האלהים את האדם ישר והמה בקשו חשבנות רבים asah haelohim eth haadam yashar vehemhah bikkeshu chishbonoth rabbim. "Elohim has made mankind upright, and they have sought many computations." "He hath meddled with endless questions." - Vulgate. "Many reasonings." - Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic. "They seek dyverse sotylties." Coverdale. <div eID="gen25573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25574" type="x-p"/> And he himself mengide with questions without eend. - Old MS. Bible. <div eID="gen25574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25575" type="x-p"/> The Targum considers the text as speaking of Adam and Eve. "This have I found out, that the Lord made the first man upright before him, and innocent: but the serpent and Eve seduced him to eat of the fruit of the tree, which gave the power to those who ate of it to discern between good and evil; and was the cause that death came upon him, and all the inhabitants of the earth; and they sought that they might find out many stratagems to bring this evil upon all the inhabitants of the world." <div eID="gen25575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25576" type="x-p"/> I doubt much whether the word חשבנות chishbonoth should be taken in a bad sense. It may signify the whole of human devices, imaginations, inventions, artifice, with all their products; arts, sciences, schemes, plans, and all that they have found out for the destruction or melioration of life. God has given man wondrous faculties; and of them he has made strange uses, and sovereign abuses: and they have been, in consequence, at one time his help, and at another his bane. This is the fair way of understanding this question.  <chapter eID="Eccl.7"/> <div eID="gen25576" type="x-p"/>

entries.acc98624fe69bee83b5ddf1365dc1800e9dc65fa: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ecc 7:1</reference> “Better is a name than precious ointment; and better is the day of death than the day when one is born.” Like ראה and ירא, so שׁם and שׁמן stand to each other in the relation of a paronomasia (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Song under Sol 1:3). Luther translates: “<hi type="italic">Ein gut Gerücht ist besser denn gute Salbe</hi>” “a good odour (= reputation) is better than good ointment. If we substitute the expression <hi type="italic">denn Wolgeruch</hi> than sweet scent, that would be the best possible rendering of the paronomasia. In the arrangement טוב ... טוב שׁם, <hi type="italic">tov</hi> would be adj. to <hi type="italic">shem</hi> (a good reputation goes beyond sweet scent); but <hi type="italic">tov</hi> standing first in the sentence is pred., and <hi type="italic">shem</hi> thus in itself alone, as in the cogn. prov., <reference osisRef="Prov.22.1">Pro 22:1</reference>, signifies a good, well-sounding, honourable, if not venerable name; cf. anshē hashshem, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.4">Gen 6:4</reference>; veli-shem, nameless, Job 30:8. The author gives the dark reverse to this bright side of the distich: the day of death better than the day in which one (a man), or he (the man), is born; cf. for this reference of the pronoun, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.12">Ecc 4:12</reference>; Ecc 5:17. It is the same lamentation as at Ecc 4:2., which sounds less strange from the mouth of a Greek than from that of an Israelite; a Thracian tribe, the Trausi, actually celebrated their birthdays as days of sadness, and the day of death as a day of rejoicing (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Bähr’s Germ. translat. of <hi type="italic">Herodotus</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.4">Ecc 4:4</reference>). - Among the people of the Old Covenant this was not possible; also a saying such as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ecc 7:1</reference></hi> is not in the spirit of the O.T. revelation of religion; yet it is significant that it was possible<note placement="foot">“The reflections of the Preacher,” says Hitzig (<hi type="italic">Süd. deut. ev. protest. Woch. Blatt</hi>, 1864, No. 2) “present the picture of a time in which men, participating in the recollection of a mighty religious past, and become sceptical by reason of the sadness of the present time, grasping here and there in uncertainty, were in danger of abandoning that stedfastness of faith which was the first mark of the religion of the prophets.”</note> within it, without apostasy from it; within the N.T. revelation of religion, except in such references as <reference osisRef="Matt.26.24">Mat 26:24</reference>, it is absolutely impossible without apostasy from it, or without rejection of its fundamental meaning.
entries.14b1f7bdd8ae6fbb3032c2dd155fffaef5dc6f12: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.2">Ecc 7:2</reference> <div eID="gen12301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12302" type="x-p"/> Still more in the spirit of the N.T. (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Luke.6.25">Luk 6:25</reference>) are these words of this singular book which stands on the border of both Testaments: “It is better to go into a house of mourning than to go into a house of carousal (drinking): for that is the end of every man; and the living layeth it to heart.” A house is meant in which there is sorrow on account of a death; the lamentation continued for seven days (Sirach 22:10), and extended sometimes, as in the case of the death of Aaron and Moses, to thirty days; the later practice distinguished the lamentations (אנינוּת) for the dead till the time of burial, and the mournings for the dead (אבלוּת), which were divided into seven and twenty-three days of greater and lesser mourning; on the return from carrying away the corpse, there was a <hi type="italic">Trostmahl</hi> (a comforting repast), to which, according as it appears to an ancient custom, those who were to be partakers of it contributed (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.7">Jer 16:7</reference>; Hos 9:4; <reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference>, <hi type="italic">funde vinum tuum et panem tuum super sepulchra justorum</hi>).<note placement="foot">Cf. Hamb. <hi type="italic">Real Encyc. für Bibel u. Talmud</hi> (1870), article “Trauer.”</note> <div eID="gen12302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12303" type="x-p"/> This feast of sorrow the above proverb leaves out of view, although also in reference to it the contrast between the “house of carousal” and “house of mourning” remains, that in the latter the drinking must be in moderation, and not to drunkenness.<note placement="foot">Maimuni’s <hi type="italic">Hilchoth Ebel</hi>, iv. 7, xiii. 8.</note> <div eID="gen12303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12304" type="x-p"/> The going into the house of mourning is certainly thought of as a visit for the purpose of showing sympathy and of imparting consolation during the first seven days of mourning (Joh 11:31).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Ibid</hi>. xiii. 2.</note> <div eID="gen12304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12305" type="x-p"/> Thus to go into the house of sorrow, and to show one’s sympathy with the mourners there, is better than to go into a house of drinking, where all is festivity and merriment; viz., because the former (that he is mourned over as dead) is the end of every man, and the survivor takes it to heart, viz., this, that he too must die. הוּא follows attractionally the gender of סוף (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.31.11">Job 31:11</reference>, Kerı̂). What is said at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">Ecc 3:13</reference> regarding כּל־ה is appropriate to the passage before us. החי is rightly vocalised; regarding the form החי, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer in the critical remarks of our ed. of <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi> under Isa 3:22. The phrase נתן אל־לב here and at <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Ecc 9:1</reference> is synon. with שׂים אל־לב, שׂים על־לב (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa 57:1</reference>) and שׂים בּלב. How this saying agrees with Koheleth’s <hi type="italic">ultimatum</hi>: There is nothing better than to eat and drink, etc. (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">Ecc 2:24</reference>, etc.), the Talmudists have been utterly perplexed to discover; Manasse ben-Israel in his <hi type="italic">Conciliador</hi> (1632) loses himself in much useless discussion.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., the English translation by Lindo (London 1842), vol. ii. pp. 306-309.</note> <div eID="gen12305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12306" type="x-p"/> The solution of the difficulty is easy. The <hi type="italic">ultimatum</hi> does not relate to an unconditional enjoyment of life, but to an enjoyment conditioned by the fear of God. When man looks death in the face, the two things occur to him, that he should make use of his brief life, but make use of it in view of the end, thus in a manner for which he is responsible before God.
entries.a975874bb31482cb615b1336bf8b8d23531aabff: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.3-Eccl.7.4">Ecc 7:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen12306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12307" type="x-p"/> The joy of life must thus be not riot and tumult, but a joy tempered with seriousness: “Better is sorrow than laughter: for with a sad countenance it is well with the heart. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools in the house of mirth.” Grief and sorrow, כּעס, whether for ourselves or occasioned by others, is better, viz., morally better, than extravagant merriment; the heart is with רע פּ (<hi type="italic">inf</hi>. as רע, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.6">Jer 7:6</reference>; cf. פן ר, <reference osisRef="Gen.40.7">Gen 40:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.2.2">Neh 2:2</reference>), a sorrowful countenance, better than with laughter, which only masks the feeling of disquiet peculiar to man, Pro 14:13. Elsewhere לב ייטב = “the heart is (may be) of good cheer,” <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Rth 3:7; Jdg 19:6; here also joyful experience is meant, but well becoming man as a religious moral being. With a sad countenance it may be far better as regards the heart than with a merry countenance in boisterous company. Luther, in the main correct, after Jerome, who on his part follows Symmachus: “The heart is made better by sorrow.” The well-being is here meant as the reflex of a moral: <hi type="italic">bene se habere</hi>. <div eID="gen12307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12308" type="x-p"/> Sorrow penetrates the heart, draws the thought upwards, purifies, transforms. Therefore is the heart of the wise in the house of sorrow; and, on the other hand, the heart of fools is in the house of joy, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the impulse of their heart goes thither, there they feel themselves at home; a house of joy is one where there are continual feasts, or where there is at the time a revelling in joy. That <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.4">Ecc 7:4</reference> is divided not by <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, but by <hi type="italic">Zakef</hi>, has its reason in this, that of the words following אבל, none consists of three syllables; cf. on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference>, חכם. From this point forward the internal relation of the contents is broken up, according to which this series of sayings as a concluding section hangs together with that containing the observations going before in <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.1">Ecc 6:1</reference>-12.
entries.565d2d28d474160ad63de6d2755f8d0c0d93cd1f: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.5-Eccl.7.6">Ecc 7:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen12308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12309" type="x-p"/> A fourth proverb of that which is better (מן טוב) presents, like the third, the fools and the wise over against each other: “Better to hear the reproof of a wise man, than that one should hear the song of fools. For like the crackling of <hi type="italic">Nesseln</hi> (nettles) under the <hi type="italic">Kessel</hi> (kettle), so the laughter of the fool: also this is vain.” As at <reference osisRef="Prov.13.1">Pro 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.10">Pro 17:10</reference>, גּערה is the earnest and severe words of the wise, which impressively reprove, emphatically warn, and salutarily alarm. שׁיר in itself means only song, to the exclusion, however, of the plaintive song; the song of fools is, if not immoral, yet morally and spiritually hollow, senseless, and unbridled madness. Instead of משּׁמע, the words מא שׁ are used, for the twofold act of hearing is divided between different subjects. A fire of thorn-twigs flickers up quickly and crackles merrily, but also exhausts itself quickly (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.12">Psa 118:12</reference>), without sufficiently boiling the flesh in the pot; whilst a log of wood, without making any noise, accomplishes this quietly and surely. <div eID="gen12309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12310" type="x-p"/> We agree with Knobel and Vaihinger in copying the paronomasia [<hi type="italic">Nessel-Kessel</hi>]. When, on the other hand, Zöckler remarks that a fire of nettles could scarcely crackle, we advise our friend to try it for once in the end of summer with a bundle of stalks of tall dry nettles. They yield a clear blaze, a quickly expiring fire, to which here, as he well remarks, the empty laughter of foolish men is compared, who are devoid of all earnestness, and of all deep moral principles of life. This laughter is vain, like that crackling. <div eID="gen12310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12311" type="x-p"/> There is a hiatus between <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Ecc 7:6</reference> and Ecc 7:7. For how <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> can be related to <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Ecc 7:6</reference> as furnishing evidence, no interpreter has as yet been able to say. Hitzig regards <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Ecc 7:6</reference></hi> as assigning a reason for <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.5">Ecc 7:5</reference>, but 6 <hi type="italic">b</hi> as a reply (as <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> containing its motive shows) to the assertion of <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.5">Ecc 7:5</reference>, - a piece of ingenious thinking which no one imitates. Elster translates: “Yet injustice befools a wise man,” being prudently silent about this “yet.” Zöckler finds, as Knobel and Ewald do, the mediating thought in this, that the vanity of fools infects and also easily befools the wise. But the subject spoken of is not the folly of fools in general, but of their singing and laughter, to which <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> has not the most remote reference. Otherwise Hengst.: “In <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference>, the reason is given why the happiness of fools is so brief; first, the <hi type="italic">mens sana</hi> is lost, and then destruction follows.” But in that case the words ought to have been כסיל יהולל; the remark, that חכם here denotes one who ought to be and might be such, is a pure volte. Ginsburg thinks that the two verses are co-ordinated by כי; that <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Ecc 7:6</reference> gives the reason for <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.5">Ecc 7:5</reference></hi>, and <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> that for <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.5">Ecc 7:5</reference></hi>, since here, by way of example, one accessible to bribery is introduced, who would act prudently in letting himself therefore be directed by a wise man. But if he had wished to be thus understood, the author would have used another word instead of חכם, 7a, and not designated both him who reproves and him who merits reproof by the one word - the former directly, the latter at least indirectly. We do not further continue the account of the many vain attempts that have been made to bring <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> into connection with <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Ecc 7:6</reference> and Ecc 7:5. Our opinion is, that <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> is the second half of a tetrastich, the first half of which is lost, which began, as is to be supposed, with <hi type="italic">tov</hi>. The first half was almost the same as <reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">Psa 37:16</reference>, or better still, as <reference osisRef="Prov.16.8">Pro 16:8</reference>, and the whole proverb stood thus: טוב מעט בּחדקה מרב תּבוּאות בּלא משׁפּט׃ [and then follows <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> as it lies before us in the text, formed into a distich, the first line of which terminates with חכם]. We go still further, and suppose that after the first half of the tetrastich was lost, that expression, “also this is vain,” added to <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.6">Ecc 7:6</reference> by the punctuation, was inserted for the purpose of forming a connection for כי עשק: Also this is vain, that, etc. (כי, like <hi type="italic">asher</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ecc 8:14</reference>).
entries.e4a6764dc67b653f7d46daa94f63c7825ecb628a: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> <div eID="gen12311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12312" type="x-p"/> Without further trying to explain the mystery of the כי, we translate this verse: “... For oppression maketh wise men mad, and corruption destroyeth the understanding.” From the lost first half of the verse, it appears that the subject here treated of is the duties of a judge, including those of a ruler into whose hands his subjects, with their property and life, are given. The second half is like an echo of <reference osisRef="Exod.23.8">Exo 23:8</reference>; Deu 16:19. That which שׁחד there means is here, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.15.27">Pro 15:27</reference>, denoted by מתּנה; and עשׁק is accordingly oppression as it is exercised by one who constrains others who need legal aid and help generally to purchase it by means of presents. Such oppression for the sake of gain, even if it does not proceed to the perversion of justice, but only aims at courting and paying for favour, makes a wise man mad (הולל, as at <reference osisRef="Job.12.17">Job 12:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.25">Isa 44:25</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it hurries him forth, since the greed of gold increases more and more, to the most blinding immorality and regardlessness; and such presents for the purpose of swaying the judgment, and of bribery, destroys the heart, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the understanding (cf. Hos 4:11, <hi type="italic">Bereschith rabba</hi>, chap. lvi.), for they obscure the judgment, blunt the conscience, and make a man the slave of his passion. The conjecture העשׁר (riches) instead of the word העשׁק (Burger, as earlier Ewald) is accordingly unnecessary; it has the parallelism against it, and thus generally used gives an untrue thought. The word הולל does not mean “gives lustre” (Desvoeux), or “makes shine forth = makes manifest” (Tyler); thus also nothing is gained for a better connection of <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference> and Ecc 7:6. The Venet. excellently: ἐκστήσει. Aben Ezra supposes that מתנה is here = דּבר מת; Mendelssohn repeats it, although otherwise the consciousness of the syntactical rule, Gesen. §147 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, does not fail him.
entries.ce3d0e0a20b3b3d9cc2a138878b5335cdf8401f5: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.8">Ecc 7:8</reference> <div eID="gen12312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12313" type="x-p"/> There now follows a fourth, or, taking into account the mutilated one, a fifth proverb of that which is better: “Better the end of a thing than its beginning; better one who forbears than one who is haughty. Hasten thyself not in thy spirit to become angry: for anger lieth down in the bosom of fools.” The clause 8 <hi type="italic">a</hi> is first thus to be objectively understood as it stands. It is not without limitation true; for of a matter in itself evil, the very contrary is true, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.4">Pro 5:4</reference>; Pro 23:32. But if a thing is not in itself evil, the end of its progress, the reaching to its goal, the completion of its destination, is always better than its beginning, which leaves it uncertain whether it will lead to a prosperous issue. An example of this is Solon’s saying to Croesus, that only he is to be pronounced happy whose good fortune it is to end his life well in the possession of his wealth (<hi type="italic">Herod</hi>. i. 32). <div eID="gen12313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12314" type="x-p"/> The proverb <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.8">Ecc 7:8</reference></hi> will stand in some kind of connection with 8 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, since what it says is further continued in Ecc 7:9. In itself, the frequently long and tedious development between the beginning and the end of a thing requires expectant patience. But if it is in the interest of a man to see the matter brought to an issue, an ארך אףּ will, notwithstanding, wait with self-control in all quietness for the end; while it lies in the nature of the רוּח גּבהּ, the haughty, to fret at the delay, and to seek to reach the end by violent means; for the haughty man thinks that everything must at once be subservient to his wish, and he measures what others should do by his own measureless self-complacency. We may with Hitzig translate: “Better is patience (ארך = ארך) than haughtiness” (גּבהּ, <hi type="italic">inf</hi>., as שׁפל, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.4">Ecc 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.19">Pro 16:19</reference>). But there exists no reason for this; גּבהּ is not to be held, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.16.5">Pro 16:5</reference>, and elsewhere generally, as the connecting form of גּבהּ, and so ארך for that of ארך; it amounts to the same thing whether the two properties (characters) or the persons possessing them are compared.
entries.23b0c9a67aee5b4092a32a1e74b9fcc78f102757: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.9">Ecc 7:9</reference> <div eID="gen12314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12315" type="x-p"/> In this verse the author warns against this pride which, when everything does not go according to its mind, falls into passionate excitement, and thoughtlessly judges, or with a violent rude hand anticipates the end. אל־תּב: do not overturn, hasten not, rush not, as at Ecc 5:1. Why the word בּרוּחך, and not בנפשך or בלבך, is used, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. pp. 197-199: passionate excitements overcome a man according to the biblical representation of his spirit, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.28">Pro 25:28</reference>, and in the proving of the spirit that which is in the heart comes forth in the mood and disposition, Pro 15:13. כּעוס is an infin., like ישׁון, Ecc 5:11. The warning has its reason in this, that anger or (כעס, taken more potentially than actually) fretfulness rests in the bosom of fools, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, is cherished and nourished, and thus is at home, and, as it were (thought of personally, as if it were a wicked demon), feels itself at home (ינוּח, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.14.33">Pro 14:33</reference>). The haughty impetuous person, and one speaking out rashly, thus acts like a fool. In fact, it is folly to let oneself be impelled by contradictions to anger, which disturbs the brightness of the soul, takes away the considerateness of judgment, and undermines the health, instead of maintaining oneself with equanimity, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, without stormy excitement, and losing the equilibrium of the soul under every opposition to our wish. <div eID="gen12315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12316" type="x-p"/> From this point the proverb loses the form “better than,” but tov still remains the catchword of the following proverbs. The proverb here first following is so far cogn., as it is directed against a particular kind of ka'as (anger), viz., discontentment with the present.
entries.babbf3023e0dd020b14e60260c862f77cf344880: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Ecc 7:10</reference> “Say not: How comes it that the former times were better than these now? for thou dost not, from wisdom, ask after this.” Cf. these lines from Horace (<hi type="italic">Poet</hi>. 173, 4):<hi type="italic">“Difficilis, querulus, laudator temporis acti Se puero, censor castigatorque minorum.”</hi> <div eID="gen12316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12317" type="x-p"/> Such an one finds the earlier days - not only the old days described in history (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.32">Deu 4:32</reference>), but also those he lived in before the present time (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.29">2Ch 9:29</reference>) - thus by contrast to much better than the present tones, that in astonishment he asks: “What is it = how comes it that?” etc. The author designates this question as one not proceeding from wisdom: מח, like the Mishnic חכמה מתּוך, and על שׁאל, as at <reference osisRef="Neh.1.2">Neh 1:2</reference>; 'al-zeh refers to that question, after the ground of the contrast, which is at the same time an exclamation of wonder. The כי, assigning a reason for the dissuasion, does not mean that the cause of the difference between the present and the good old times is easily seen; but it denotes that the supposition of this difference is foolish, because in truth every age has its bright and its dark sides; and this division of light and shadow between the past and the present betrays a want of understanding of the signs of the times and of the ways of God. This proverb does not furnish any point of support for the determination of the date of the authorship of the Book of Koheleth. But if it was composed in the last century of the Persian domination, this dissatisfaction with the present times is explained, over against which Koheleth leads us to consider that it is self-deception and one-sidedness to regard the present as all dark and the past as all bright and rosy.
entries.1540e2495cc9f94b5092c02a1d958b3e07567a2d: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.11-Eccl.7.12">Ecc 7:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen12317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12318" type="x-p"/> Externally connecting itself with “from wisdom,” there now follows another proverb, which declares that wisdom along with an inheritance is good, but that wisdom is nevertheless of itself better than money and possessions: “Wisdom is good with family possessions, and an advantage for those who see the sun. For wisdom affordeth a shadow, money affordeth a shadow; yet the advantage of knowledge is this, that wisdom preserveth life to its possessor.” Most of the English interpreters, from Desvoeux to Tyler, translate: “Wisdom is as good as an inheritance;” and Bullock, who translates: “with an inheritance,” says of this and the other translations: “The difference is not material.” But the thought is different, and thus the distinction is not merely a formal one. Zöckl. explains it as undoubted that עם here, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.16">Ecc 2:16</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>), means <hi type="italic">aeque ac</hi>; (but (1) that <hi type="italic">aeque ac</hi> has occurred to no ancient translator, till the Venet. and Luther, nor to the Syr., which translates: “better is wisdom than weapons (מאנא זינא),” in a singular way making <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.11">Ecc 7:11</reference></hi> a duplette of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">Ecc 9:18</reference></hi>; (2) instead of “wisdom is better than wealth,” as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.11">Pro 8:11</reference>; (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.3">3</reference>) the proverb is formed like <hi type="italic">Aboth</hi> ii. 2, “good is study connected with a citizen-like occupation,” and similar proverbs; (4) one may indeed say: “the wise man dieth with (together with) the fool” = just as well as the fool; but “good is wisdom with wealth” can neither be equivalent to “as well as wealth,” nor: “in comparison with wealth” (Ewald, Elster), but only: “in connection with wealth (possessions);” <hi type="italic">aeque ac</hi> may be translated for <hi type="italic">una cum</hi> where the subject is common action and suffering, but not in a substantival clause consisting of a subst. as subject and an adj. as pred., having the form of a categorical judgment. נחלה denotes a possession inherited and hereditary (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.20.21">Pro 20:21</reference>); and this is evidence in favour of the view that עם is meant not of comparison, but of connection; the expression would otherwise be עם־עשׁר. ויתר is now also explained. It is not to be rendered: “and better still” (than wealth), as Herzf., Hitz., and Hengst. render it; but in spite of Hengst., who decides in his own way, “יותר never means advantage, gain,” it denotes a prevailing good, <hi type="italic">avantage</hi>; and it is explained also why men are here named “those who see the sun” - certainly not merely thus describing them poetically, as in Homer ζώειν is described and coloured by ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο. To see the sun, is = to have entered upon this earthly life, in which along with wisdom, also no inheritance is to be despised. For wisdom affords protection as well as money, but the former still more than the latter. So far, the general meaning of <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.12">Ecc 7:12</reference> is undisputed. Buthow is <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.12">Ecc 7:12</reference></hi> to be construed? Knobel, Hitz., and others regard ב as the so-called <hi type="italic">beth essentiae</hi>: a shadow (protection) is wisdom, a shadow is money, - very expressive, yet out of harmony, if not with the language of that period, yet with the style of Koheleth; and how useless and misleading would this doubled בּ be here! Hengstenberg translates: in the shadow of wisdom, at least according to our understanding of <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.11">Ecc 7:11</reference>, is not likened to the shadow of silver; but in conformity with that עם, it must be said that wisdom, and also that money, affords a shadow; (2) but that interpretation goes quite beyond the limits of gnomic brachyology. We explain: for in the shadow (בּצל, like בּצּל, <reference osisRef="Jonah.4.5">Jon 4:5</reference>) is wisdom, in the shadow, money; by which, without any particularly bold poetic licence, is meant that he who possesses wisdom, he who possesses money, finds himself in a shadow, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of pleasant security; to be in the shadow, spoken of wisdom and money, is = to sit in the shadow of the persons who possess both. 12b. The exposition of this clause is agreed upon. It is to be construed according to the accentuation: and the advantage of knowledge is this, that “wisdom preserveth life to its possessors.” The Targ. regards דעת החכמה as connected genit.; that might be possible (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">Ecc 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.16">Ecc 8:16</reference>), but yet is improbable. Wherever the author uses דעת as subst., it is an independent conception placed beside חך, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.16">Ecc 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Ecc 2:26</reference>, etc. We now translate, not: wisdom gives life (lxx, Jerome, Venet., Luther) to its possessors; for חיּה always means only either to revive (thus Hengst., after <reference osisRef="Ps.119.25">Psa 119:25</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.71.20">Psa 71:20</reference>) or to keep in life; and this latter meaning is more appropriate to this book than the former, - thus (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Pro 3:18</reference>): wisdom preserves in life, - since, after Hitzig, it accomplishes this, not by rash utterances of denunciation, - a thought lying far behind <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Ecc 7:10</reference>, and altogether too mean, - but since it secures it against self-destruction by vice and passions and emotions, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, anger (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.9">Ecc 7:9</reference>), which consume life. The shadow in which wisdom (the wise man) sits keeps it fresh and sound, - a result which the shadow in which money (the capitalist) sits does not afford: it has frequently the directly contrary effect.
entries.478898a250da725d9ff5b400dd38e050fa7b8f3f: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.13-Eccl.7.14">Ecc 7:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen12318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12319" type="x-p"/> There now follows a proverb of devout submission to the providence of God, connecting itself with the contents of <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Ecc 7:10</reference> : “Consider the work of God: for who can make that straight which He hath made crooked! In the good day be of good cheer, and in the day of misfortune observe: God hath also made this equal to that, to the end that man need not experience anything (further) after his death.” While ראה, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.10">Ecc 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.27">Ecc 7:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.29">Ecc 7:29</reference>, is not different from הנּה, and in <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.9">Ecc 9:9</reference> has the meaning of “enjoy,” here the meaning of contemplative observation, mental seeing, connects itself both times with it. כּי before מי can as little mean <hi type="italic">quod</hi>, as <hi type="italic">asher</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ecc 6:12</reference>, before <hi type="italic">mi</hi> can mean <hi type="italic">quoniam</hi>. “Consider God’s work” means: recognise in all that is done the government of God, which has its motive in this, that, as the question leads us to suppose, no creature is able (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">Ecc 6:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.15">Ecc 1:15</reference>) to put right God’s work in cases where it seems to contradict that which is right (<reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.12">Job 34:12</reference>), or to make straight that which He has made crooked (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.9">Psa 146:9</reference>). 14a. The call here expressed is parallel to Sir. 14:14 (Fritz.): “Withdraw not thyself from a good day, and let not thyself lose participation in a right enjoyment.” The ב of בּטובis, as little as that of בּצל, the <hi type="italic">beth essentiae</hi> - it is not a designation of quality, but of condition: in good, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, cheerful mood. He who is, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer 44:17</reference>, personally <hi type="italic">tov</hi>, cheerful (= <hi type="italic">tov lev</hi>), is betov (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.25.13">Psa 25:13</reference>, also <reference osisRef="Job.21.13">Job 21:13</reference>). The reverse side of the call, 14 <hi type="italic">a</hi>b, is of course not to be translated: and suffer or bear the bad day (Ewald, Heiligst.), for in this sense we use the expression רעה ראה, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer 44:17</reference>, but not ברעה ראה, which much rather, Oba 1:13, means a malicious contemplation of the misfortune of a stranger, although once, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.16">Gen 21:16</reference>, ב ראה also occurs in the sense of a compassionate, sympathizing look, and, moreover, the parall. shows that רעה ביום is not the obj., but the adv. designation of time. Also not: look to = be attentive to (Salomon), or bear it patiently (Burger), for ראה cannot of itself have that meaning.<note placement="foot">Similarly also Sohar (Par. (מחור): הוי וגו, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">cave et circumspice</hi>, viz., that thou mayest not incur the judgment which is pronounced.</note> <div eID="gen12319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12320" type="x-p"/> But: in the day of misfortune observe, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, perceive and reflect: God has also made (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.2.10">Job 2:10</reference>) the latter לעמּת corresponding, parallel, like to (cf. under <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.15">Ecc 5:15</reference>) the former. <div eID="gen12320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12321" type="x-p"/> So much the more difficult is the statement of the object of this mingling by God of good and evil in the life of man. It is translated: that man may find nothing behind him; this is literal, but it is meaningless. The meaning, according to most interpreters, is this: that man may investigate nothing that lies behind his present time, - thus, that belongs to the future; in other words: that man may never know what is before him. But aharav is never (not at <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ecc 6:12</reference>) = in the future, lying out from the present of a man; but always = after his present life. Accordingly, Ewald explains, and Heiligst. with him: that he may find nothing which, dying, he could take with him. But this rendering (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.14">Ecc 5:14</reference>) is here unsuitable. Better, Hitzig: because God wills it that man shall be rid of all things after his death, He puts evil into the period of his life, and lets it alternate with good, instead of visiting him therewith after his death. This explanation proceeds from a right interpretation of the words: idcirco ut (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.18">Ecc 3:18</reference>) <hi type="italic">non inveniat homo post se quidquam, scil. quod non expertus sit</hi>, but gives a meaning to the expression which the author would reject as unworthy of his conception of God. What is meant is much more this, that God causes man to experience good and evil that he may pass through the whole school of life, and when he departs hence that nothing may be outstanding (in arrears) which he has not experienced.
entries.a48e7ba7b112ca13d0fdeb0caeabd36f8f09f57d: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15-Eccl.7.16">Ecc 7:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen12321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12322" type="x-p"/> The first of these counsels warns against extremes, on the side of good as well as on that of evil: “All have I seen in the days of my vanity: there are righteous men who perish by their righteousness, and there are wicked men who continue long by their wickedness. Be not righteous over-much, and show not thyself wise beyond measure: why wilt thou ruin thyself? Be not wicked overmuch, and be no fool: why wilt thou die before thy time is? It is good that thou holdest thyself to the one, and also from the other withdrawest not thine hand: for he that feareth God accomplisheth it all.” One of the most original English interpreters of the Book of <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi>, T. Tyler (1874), finds in the thoughts of the book - composed, according to his view, about 200 b.c. - and in their expression, references to the post-Aristotelian philosophy, particularly to the Stoic, variously interwoven with orientalism. But here, in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15-Eccl.7.18">Ecc 7:15-18</reference>, we perceive, not so much the principle of the Stoical ethics - τῇ φύσει ὁμολογουμένως ζῆν - as that of the Aristotelian, according to which virtue consists in the art μέσως ἔξηειν, the art of holding the middle between extremes.<note placement="foot">Cf. Luthardt’s <hi type="italic">Lectures on the Moral Truths of Christianity</hi>, 2nd ed. Edin., T. and T. Clark.</note> <div eID="gen12322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12323" type="x-p"/> Also, we do not find here a reference to the contrasts between Pharisaism and Sadduceeism (Zöckl.), viz., those already in growth in the time of the author; for if it should be also true, as Tyler conjectures, that the Sadducees had such a predilection for Epicurism, - as, according to Josephus (<hi type="italic">Vit</hi>. c. 2), “the doctrine of the Pharisees is of kin to that of the Stoics,” - yet צדקה and רשׁעה are not apportioned between these two parties, especially since the overstraining of conformity to the law by the Pharisees related not to the moral, but to the ceremonial law. We derive nothing for the right understanding of the passage from referring the wisdom of life here recommended to the tendencies of the time. The author proceeds from observation, over against which the O.T. saints knew not how to place any satisfying theodicee. הבלי ימי (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ecc 6:12</reference>) he so designates the long, but for the most part uselessly spent life lying behind him. 'et-hakol is not “everything possible” (Zöckl.), but “all, of all kinds” (Luth.), which is defined by 15 <hi type="italic">b</hi> as of two kinds; for 15 <hi type="italic">a</hi> is the introduction of the following experience relative to the righteous and the unrighteous, and thus to the two classes into which all men are divided. We do not translate: there are the righteous, who by their righteousness, etc. (Umbr., Hitzig, and others); for if the author should thus commence, it would appear as if he wished to give unrighteousness the preference to righteousness, which, however, was far from him. To perish in or by his righteousness, to live long in or by his wickedness (מאריך, <hi type="italic">scil</hi>. ימים, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.13">Ecc 8:13</reference>, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.28.2">Pro 28:2</reference>), is = to die in spite of righteousness, to live in spite of wickedness, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.32">Deu 1:32</reference> : “in this thing” = in spite of, etc. Righteousness has the promise of long life as its reward; but if this is the rule, it has yet its exceptions, and the author thence deduces the doctrine that one should not exaggerate righteousness; for if it occurs that a righteous man, in spite of his righteousness, perishes, this happens, at earliest, in the case in which, in the practice of righteousness, he goes beyond the right measure and limit. The relative conceptions הרבּה and יותר have here, since they are referred to the idea of the right measure, the meaning of <hi type="italic">nimis</hi>. חתחכּם could mean, “to play the wise man;” but that, whether more or less done, is objectionable. It means, as at <reference osisRef="Exod.1.10">Exo 1:10</reference>, to act wisely (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.105.25">Psa 105:25</reference>, הת, to act cunningly). And השׁ, which is elsewhere used of being inwardly torpid, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, being astonished, <hi type="italic">obstupescere</hi>, has here the meaning of placing oneself in a benumbed, disordered state, or also, passively, of becoming disconcerted; not of becoming desolate or being deserted (Hitz., Ginsburg, and others), which it could only mean in highly poetic discourse (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa 54:1</reference>). The form תּשּׁומם is syncop., like תּךּ, Num 21:27; and the question, with למּה, here and at <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.17">Ecc 7:17</reference></hi>, is of the same kind as <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.5">Ecc 5:5</reference>; Luther, weakening it: “that thou mayest not destroy thyself.”
