entries.0337be6fc26509f1d16ec17ff2f257e549001100: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.17">Ecc 7:17</reference> <div eID="gen12323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12324" type="x-p"/> Up to this point all is clear: righteousness and wisdom are good and wholesome, and worth striving for; but even in these a transgressing of the right measure is possible (Luther remembers the <hi type="italic">summum just summa injuria</hi>), which has as a consequence, that they become destructive to man, because he thereby becomes a caricature, and either perishes rushing from one extreme into another, or is removed out of the way by others whose hatred he provokes. But it is strange that the author now warns against an excess in wickedness, so that he seems to find wickedness, up to a certain degree, praiseworthy and advisable. So much the stranger, since “be no fool” stands as contrast to “show not thyself wise,” etc.; so that “but also be no wicked person” was much rather to be expected as contrast to “be not righteous over-much.” Zöckler seeks to get over this difficulty with the remark: “Koheleth does not recommend a certain moderation in wickedness as if he considered it allowable, but only because he recognises the fact as established, that every man is by nature somewhat wicked.” The meaning would then be: man’s life is not free from wickedness, but be only not too wicked! The offensiveness of the advice is not thus removed; and besides, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ecc 7:18</reference></hi> demands in a certain sense, an intentional wickedness, - indeed, as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ecc 7:18</reference></hi> shows, a wickedness in union with the fear of God. The correct meaning of “be not wicked over-much” may be found if for תרשׁע we substitute תּחטא; in this form the good counsel at once appears as impossible, for it would be immoral, since “sinning,” in all circumstances, is an act which carries in itself its own sentence of condemnation. Thus רשׁע must here be a setting oneself free from the severity of the law, which, although sin in the eyes of the over-righteous, is yet no sin in itself; and the author here thinks, in accordance with the spirit of his book, principally of that fresh, free, joyous life to which he called the young, that joy of life in its fulness which appeared to him as the best and fairest reality in this present time; but along with that, perhaps also of transgressions of the letter of the law, of shaking off the scruples of conscience which conformity to God-ordained circumstances brings along with it. He means to say: be not a narrow rigorist, - enjoy life, accommodate thyself to life; but let not the reins be too loose; and be no fool who wantonly places himself above law and discipline: Why wilt thou destroy thy life before the time by suffering vice to kill thee (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.22">Psa 34:22</reference>), and by want of understanding ruin thyself (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.21">Pro 10:21</reference>)?<note placement="foot">An old proverb, <hi type="italic">Sota</hi> 3a, says: “A man commits no transgression unless there rules in him previously the spirit of folly.”</note>
entries.8fa0d8646addb5ebdd42dfbe5ddef64b8d38891b: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">Ecc 7:18</reference> “It is good that thou holdest fast to the one,” - viz. righteousness and wisdom, - and withdrawest not thy hand from the other, - viz. a wickedness which renounces over-righteousness and over-wisdom, or an unrestrained life; - for he who fears God accomplishes all, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, both, the one as well as the other. Luther, against the Vulg.: “for he who fears God escapes all.” But what “all”? Tyler, Bullock, and others reply: “All the perplexities of life;” but no such thing is found in the text here, however many perplexities may be in the book. Better, Zöckler: the evil results of the extreme of false righteousness as of bold wickedness. But that he does not destroy himself and does not die before his time, is yet only essentially one thing which he escapes; also, from <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ecc 7:15</reference>, only one thing, אבד, is taken. Thus either: the extremes (Umbr.), or: the extremes together with their consequences. The thought presents a connected, worthy conclusion. But if ěth-kullam, with its retrospective suffix, can be referred to that which immediately precedes, this ought to have the preference. Ginsburg, with Hitzig: “Whoso feareth God will make his way with both;” but what an improbable phrase! Jerome, with his vague nihil negligit, is right as to the meaning. In the Bible, the phrase ה ... יחא, <hi type="italic">egressus est urbem</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.44.4">Gen 44:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.10.20">Jer 10:20</reference>, is used; and in the Mishna, יצא את־ידי חובתו, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he has discharged his duty, he is quit of it by fulfilling it. For the most part, יצא merely is used: he has satisfied his duty; and יצא לא, he has not satisfied it, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 2:1. Accordingly יחא - since ěth-kullam relates to, “these ought he to have done, and not to leave the other undone,” <reference osisRef="Matt.23.23">Mat 23:23</reference> - here means: he who fears God will set himself free from all, will acquit himself of the one as well as of the other, will perform both, and thus preserve the golden via media.
entries.f112167e727e3cf27db54db568bbe3ad6bccce49: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ecc 7:19</reference> “Wisdom affords strong protection to the wise man more than ten mighty men who are in the city.” We have to distinguish, as is shown under <reference osisRef="Ps.31.3">Psa 31:3</reference>, the verbs עזז, to be strong, and עוּז, to flee for refuge; תּעז is the fut. of the former, whence מעז, stronghold, safe retreat, protection, and with ל, since עזז means not only to be strong, but also to show oneself strong, as at Eccl 9:20, to feel and act as one strong; it has also the trans. meaning, to strengthen, as shown in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Psa 68:29</reference>, but here the intrans. suffices: wisdom proves itself strong for the wise man. The ten <hi type="italic">shallithim</hi> are not, with Ginsburg, to be multiplied indefinitely into “many mighty men.” And it is not necessary, with Desvoeux, Hitz., Zöckl., and others, to think of ten chiefs (commanders of forces), including the portions of the city garrison which they commanded. The author probably in this refers to some definite political arrangement, perhaps to the ten archons, like those Assyrian salaṭ, vice-regents, after whom as eponyms the year was named by the Greeks. שׁלּיט, in the Asiatic kingdom, was not properly a military title. And did a town then need protection only in the time of war, and not also at other times, against injury threatening its trade, against encroachments on its order, against the spread of infectious diseases, against the force of the elements? As the Deutero-Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.17">Isa 60:17</reference>) says of Jerusalem: “I will make thy officers peace, and thine exactors righteousness,” so <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi> says here that wisdom affords a wise man as strong a protection as a powerful decemvirate a city; cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Prov.24.5">Pro 24:5</reference></hi>: “A wise man is ba'oz,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, mighty.
entries.87b0904216525d4c9fa688c58e78b596d79feb62: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.20">Ecc 7:20</reference> “For among men there is not a righteous man on the earth, who doeth good, and sinneth not.” The original passage, found in Solomon’s prayer at the consecration of the temple, is briefer, 1Ki 8:46 : “There is no man who sinneth not.” Here the words might be וגו צדּיק אדם אין, there is no righteous man ... . <hi type="italic">Adam</hi> stands here as representing the species, as when we say in Germ.: <hi type="italic">Menschen gibt es keine gerechten auf Erden</hi> [men, there are none righteous on earth]; cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.5.16">Exo 5:16</reference> : “Straw, none was given.” The verification of <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ecc 7:19</reference> by reference to the fact of the common sinfulness from which even the most righteous cannot free himself, does not contradict all expectation to the same degree as the <hi type="italic">ki</hi> in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference>; but yet it surprises us, so that Mercer and Grätz, with Aben Ezra, take <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.20">Ecc 7:20</reference> as the verification of <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ecc 7:16</reference>, here first adduced, and Knobel and Heiligst. and others connect it with <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.21">Ecc 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.22">Ecc 7:22</reference>, translating: “Because there is not a just man ... , therefore it is also the part of wisdom to take no heed unto all words,” etc. But these are all forced interpretations; instead of the latter, we would rather suppose that <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.20">Ecc 7:20</reference> originally stood after <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.22">Ecc 7:22</reference>, and is separated from its correct place. But yet the sequence of thought lying before us may be conceived, and that not merely as of necessity, but as that which was intended by the author. On the whole, Hitzig is correct: “For every one, even the wise man, sins; in which case virtue, which has forsaken him, does not protect him, but wisdom proves itself as his means of defence.” Zöckler adds: “against the judicial justice of God;” but one escapes from this by a penitent appeal to grace, for which there is no need for the personal property of wisdom; there is thus reason rather for thinking on the dangerous consequences which often a single false step has for a man in other respects moral; in the threatening complications in which he is thereby involved, it is wisdom which then protects him and delivers him. Otherwise Tyler, who by the עז, which the wise has in wisdom, understands power over evil, which is always moving itself even in the righteous. But the sinning spoken of in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.20">Ecc 7:20</reference> is that which is unavoidable, which even wisdom cannot prevent or make inefficacious. On the contrary, it knows how to prevent the destruction which threatens man from his transgressions, and to remove the difficulties and derangements which thence arise. The good counsel following is connected by <hi type="italic">gam</hi> with the foregoing. The exhortation to strive after wisdom, contained in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ecc 7:19</reference>, which affords protection against the evil effects of the failures which run through the life of the righteous, is followed by the exhortation, that one conscious that he himself is not free from transgression, should take heed to avoid that tale-bearing which finds pleasure in exposing to view the shortcomings of others.
entries.b20c1a1400d497a7a162dddf063e54d5a9c56ef7: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.21-Eccl.7.22">Ecc 7:21-22</reference> “Also give not thy heart to all the words which one speaketh, lest thou shouldest hear thy servant curse thee. For thy heart knoweth in many cases that thou also hast cursed others.” The talk of the people, who are the indef. subj. of ילבּרוּ (lxx, Targ., Syr. supply ἀσεβεῖς), is not about “thee who givest heed to the counsels just given” (Hitz., Zöckl.), for the restrictive עליך is wanting; and why should a servant be zealous to utter imprecations on the conduct of his master, which rests on the best maxims? It is the babbling of the people in general that is meant. To this one ought not to turn his heart (ל ... נתן, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ecc 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">Ecc 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ecc 8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.16">Ecc 8:16</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, gives wilful attention, <hi type="italic">ne</hi> (לא אשׁר = פּן, which does not occur in the Book of Koheleth) <hi type="italic">audias servum tuum tibi maledicere</hi>; the particip. expression of the pred. obj. follows the analogy of <reference osisRef="Gen.21.9">Gen 21:9</reference>, Ewald, §284 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and is not a Graecism; for since in this place hearing is meant, not immediately, but mediated through others, the expression would not in good Greek be with the lxx ... τοῦ δούλου σου καταρωμένου σε, but τὸν δοῦλόν σου καταρᾶσθαι σε. The warning has its motive in this, that by such roundabout hearing one generally hears most unpleasant things; and on hearsay no reliance can be placed. Such gossiping one should ignore, should not listen to it at all; and if, nevertheless, something so bad is reported as that our own servant has spoken words of imprecation against us, yet we ought to pass that by unheeded, well knowing that we ourselves have often spoken harsh words against others. The expression וגו ידע, “thou art conscious to thyself that,” is like פּע ר, 1Ki 2:44, not the obj. accus. dependent on ידע (Hitz.), “many cases where also thou ...,” but the adv. accus. of time to קּלּלתּ; the words are inverted (Ewald, §336 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), the style of Koheleth being fond of thus giving prominence to the chief conception (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.20">Ecc 7:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">Ecc 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">Ecc 3:13</reference>). The first <hi type="italic">gam</hi>, although it belongs to “thine, thy,” as at <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.22">Ecc 7:22</reference></hi> it is also connected with “thou,”<note placement="foot">גּם־אתּ, on account of the half pause, accented on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. according to the Masora.</note> stands at the beginning of the sentence, after such syntactical examples as Hos 6:11; Zec 9:11; and even with a two-membered sentence, Job 2:10.
entries.4d813d892e02f2c7cc0081b7bafb1f8433db45be: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.23">Ecc 7:23</reference> “All this have I proved by wisdom: I thought, Wise I will become; but it remained far from me.” The ב in בּחכמה is, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ecc 1:13</reference>, that designating the <hi type="italic">organon</hi>, the means of knowledge. Thus he possessed wisdom up to a certain degree, and in part; but his purpose, comprehended in the one word אחכּמה, was to possess it fully and completely; <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, not merely to be able to record observations and communicate advices, but to adjust the contradictions of life, to expound the mysteries of time and eternity, and generally to solve the most weighty and important questions which perplex men. But this wisdom was for him still in the remote distance. It is the wisdom after which Job, chap. 28, made inquiry in all regions of the world and at all creatures, at last to discover that God has appointed to man only a limited share of wisdom. <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi> briefly condenses <reference osisRef="Job.28.12-Job.28.22">Job 28:12-22</reference> in the words following:
entries.835295b2be4e2cf868a098f45f0b5e3a3fec66ef: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.24">Ecc 7:24</reference> “For that which is, is far off, and deep, - yes, deep; who can reach it?” Knobel, Hitz., Vaih., and Bullock translate: for what is remote and deep, deep, who can find it? <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, investigate it; but mah-shehayah is everywhere an idea by itself, and means either <hi type="italic">id quod fuit</hi>, or <hi type="italic">id quod exstitit</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ecc 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.15">Ecc 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">Ecc 6:10</reference>; in the former sense it is the contrast of mah-shěihyěh, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.7">Ecc 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.14">Ecc 10:14</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ecc 3:22</reference>; in the latter, it is the contrast of that which does not exist, because it has not come into existence. In this way it is also not to be translated: For it is far off what it (wisdom) is (Zöckl.) [= what wisdom is lies far off from human knowledge], or: what it is (the essence of wisdom), is far off (Elst.) - which would be expressed by the words מה־שּׁהיא. And if מה־שׁהיה is an idea complete in itself, it is evidently not that which is past that is meant (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Rosenm. <hi type="italic">quod ante aderat</hi>), for that is a limitation of the obj. of knowledge, which is unsuitable here, but that which has come into existence. Rightly, Hengst.: that which has being, for wisdom is τῶν ὄντων γνῶσις ἀψευδής, Wisd. 7:17. He compares Jdg 3:11, “the work which God does,” and <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ecc 8:17</reference>, “the work which is done under the sun.” What Koheleth there says of the totality of the historical, he here says of the world of things: this (in its essence and its grounds) remains far off from man; it is for him, and also in itself and for all creatures, far too deep (עמק עמק, the ancient expression for the superlative): Who can intelligibly reach (ימץ, from מצא, <hi type="italic">assequi</hi>, in an intellectual sense, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ecc 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ecc 8:17</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Job.11.7">Job 11:7</reference>) it (this all of being)? The author appears in the book as a teacher of wisdom, and emphatically here makes confession of the limitation of his wisdom; for the consciousness of this limitation comes over him in the midst of his teaching.
entries.d5ffbd8b83583922ecfb46ab61d7ac8fbed81608: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.25">Ecc 7:25</reference> <div eID="gen12324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12325" type="x-p"/> But, on the other side, he can bear testimony to himself that he has honestly exercised himself in seeking to go to the foundation of things: “I turned myself, and my heart was there to discern, and to explore, and to seek wisdom, and the account, and to perceive wickedness as folly, and folly as madness.” Regarding sabbothi, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.20">Ecc 2:20</reference> : a turning is meant to the theme as given in what follows, which, as we have to suppose, was connected with a turning away form superficiality and frivolity. Almost all interpreters-as also the accentuation does - connect the two words ולבּי אני; but “I and my heart” is so unpsychological an expression, without example, that many Codd. (28 of Kennicott, 44 of de Rossi) read בּלבּי daer )i with my heart. The erasure of the <hi type="italic">vav</hi> (as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Luther: “I applied my heart”) would at the same time require the change of סבותי into הסבּותי. The Targ., Jerome, and the Venet. render the word בלבי; the lxx and Syr., on the contrary, ולבי; and this also is allowable, if we place the disjunctive on אני and take ולבי as consequent: my heart, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, my striving and effort, was to discern (Aben Ezra, Herzf., Stuart), - a substantival clause instead of the verbal את־לבּי ונתתּי, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ecc 1:13</reference>, Ecc 1:17. Regarding <hi type="italic">tur</hi> in an intellectual sense, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Ecc 1:13. Hhěshbon, with hhochmah, we have translated by “<hi type="italic">Rechenschaft</hi>” account, <hi type="italic">ratio</hi>; for we understand by it a knowledge well grounded and exact, and able to be established, - the <hi type="italic">facit</hi> of a calculation of all the facts and circumstances relating thereto; נתן חשׁבין is Mishnic, and = the N.T. λόγον ἀποδιδόναι. Of the two accus. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.25">Ecc 7:25</reference></hi> following לדעת, the first, as may be supposed, and as the determination in the second member shows, is that of the obj., the second that of the pred. (Ewald, §284 <hi type="italic">b</hi>): that רשׁע, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, conduct separating from God and from the law of that which is good, is kěsěl, <hi type="italic">Thorheit</hi>, folly (since, as Socrates also taught, all sinning rests on a false calculation, to the sinner’s own injury); and that hassichluth, <hi type="italic">Narrheit</hi>, foolishness, stultitia (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., sachal, and <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">Ecc 1:17</reference>), is to be thus translated (in contradistinction to כּסל), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, an intellectual and moral obtuseness, living for the day, rising up into foolery, not different from holeloth, fury, madness, and thus like a physical malady, under which men are out of themselves, rage, and are mad. Koheleth’s striving after wisdom thus, at least is the second instance (ולדעת), with a renunciation of the transcendental, went towards a practical end. And now he expresses by ומוצא one of the experiences he had reached in this way of research. How much value he attaches to this experience is evident from the long preface, by means of which it is as it were distilled. We see him there on the way to wisdom, to metaphysical wisdom, if we may so speak - it remains as far off from him as he seeks to come near to it. We then see him, yet not renouncing the effort after wisdom, on the way toward practical wisdom, which exercises itself in searching into the good and the bad; and that which has presented itself to him as the bitterest of the bitter is - a woman.
entries.f2e2ee9269a0bfb8f822b4111ba6786dbd2f2adc: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ecc 7:26</reference> “And I found woman more bitter than death; she is like hunting-nets. and like snares is her heart, her hands are bands: he who pleaseth God will escape from her; but the sinner is caught by them.” As א ושׁ, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.2">Ecc 4:2</reference>, so here וּם א gains by the preceding אני וסבּותי a past sense;<note placement="foot">With reference to this passage and <reference osisRef="Prov.18.22">Pro 18:22</reference>, it was common in Palestine when one was married to ask מצא או מוחא = happy or unhappy? Jebamoth 63 <hi type="italic">b</hi>.</note> the particip. clause stands frequently thus, not only as a circumstantial clause, Gen 14:12., but also as principal clause, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.10">Gen 2:10</reference>, in an historical connection. The preceding pred. מר, in the mas. ground-form, follows the rule, Gesen. §147. Regarding the construction of the relative clause, Hitzig judges quite correctly: “היא is copula between subj. and pred., and precedes for the sake of the contrast, giving emphasis to the pred. It cannot be a nomin., which would be taken up by the suff. in לבהּ, since if this latter were subject also to מץ, היא would not certainly be found. Also <hi type="italic">asher</hi> here is not a conj.” This הוּא (היא), which in relative substantival clauses represents the copula, for the most part stands separated from <hi type="italic">asher</hi>, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.7.2">Gen 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.17.12">Gen 17:12</reference>; Num 17:5; <reference osisRef="Deut.17.15">Deu 17:15</reference>; less frequently immediately with it, Num 35:31; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.19">1Sa 10:19</reference>; 2Ki 25:19; <reference osisRef="Lev.11.26">Lev 11:26</reference>; Deu 20:20. But this <hi type="italic">asher hu</hi> (<hi type="italic">hi</hi>) never represents the subj., placed foremost and again resumed by the reflex. pronoun, so as to be construed as the accentuation requires: <hi type="italic">quae quidem retia et laquei cor ejus</hi> = <hi type="italic">cajus quidem cor sunt retia et laquei</hi> (Heiligst.). מצוד is the means of searching, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, either of hunting: hunting-net (mitsodah, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">Ecc 9:12</reference>), or of blockading: siege-work, bulwarks, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.14">Ecc 9:14</reference>; here it is the plur. of the word in the former meaning. חרם, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.14">Hab 1:14</reference>, plur. <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">Eze 26:5</reference>, etc. (perhaps from חרם, to pierce, bore through), is one of the many synon. for fishing-net. אסוּרים, fetters, the hands (arms) of voluptuous embrace. The primary form, after <reference osisRef="Jer.37.15">Jer 37:15</reference>, is אסוּר, אסוּר; cf. אבוּס, אב, Job 39:9. Of the three clauses following <hi type="italic">asher</hi>, <hi type="italic">vav</hi> is found in the second and is wanting to the third, as at <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.9">Job 42:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.13">Isa 1:13</reference>; cf. on the other hand, Isa 33:6. Similar in their import are these Leonine verses:<hi type="italic">Femina praeclara facie quasi pestis amara, Et quasi fermentum corrumpit cor sapientum.</hi> <div eID="gen12325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12326" type="x-p"/> That the author is in full earnest in this harsh judgment regarding woman, is shown by 26 <hi type="italic">b</hi>: he who appears to God as good (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Ecc 2:26</reference>) escapes from her (the fut. of the consequence of this his relation to God); but the sinner (חוטאו) is caught by her, or, properly, in her, viz., the net-like woman, or the net to which she is compared (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.18">Isa 24:18</reference>). The harsh judgment is, however, not applicable to woman as such, but to woman as she is, with only rare exceptions; among a thousand women he has not found one corresponding to the idea of a woman.
entries.79f2f7427c9467d3b1ae68a805cdec2a44f820ca: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.27-Eccl.7.28">Ecc 7:27-28</reference> “Behold what I have found, saith Koheleth, adding one thing to another, to find out the account: What my soul hath still sought, and I have not found, (is this): one man among a thousand have I found; and a woman among all these have I not found.” It is the ascertained result, “one man, etc.,” which is solemnly introduced by the words preceding. Instead of אם קה, the words ראמר הקּה are to be read, after <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.8">Ecc 12:8</reference>, as is now generally acknowledged; errors of transcription of a similar kind are found at <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.2">2Sa 5:2</reference>; Job 38:12. Ginsburg in vain disputes this, maintaining that the name <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi>, as denoting wisdom personified, may be regarded as fem. as well as mas.; here, where the female sex is so much depreciated, was the fem. self-designation of the stern judge specially unsuitable. Hengst. supposes that <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi> is purposely fem. in this one passage, since true wisdom, represented by Solomon, stands opposite to false philosophy. But this reason for the fem. rests on the false opinion that woman here is heresy personified; he further remarks that it is significant for this fem. personification, that there is “no writing of female authorship in the whole canon of the O.T. and N.T.” But what of Deborah’s triumphal song, the song of Hannah, the <hi type="italic">magnificat</hi> of Mary? We hand this absurdity over to the Clementines! The woman here was flesh and blood, but <hi type="italic">pulchra quamvis pellis est mens tamen plean procellis</hi>; and <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi> is not incarnate wisdom, but the official name of a preacher, as in Assyr., for חזּנרם, curators, overseers, hazanâti<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Fried. Delitzsch’s <hi type="italic">Assyr. Stud</hi>. (1874), p. 132.</note> is used. זה, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.27">Ecc 7:27</reference></hi>, points, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.10">Ecc 1:10</reference>, to what follows. אחת ל, one thing to another (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Isa 27:12</reference>), must have been, like <hi type="italic">summa summarum</hi> and the like, a common arithmetical and dialectical formula, which is here subordinate to מצא, since an adv. inf. such as לקוח is to be supplemented: taking one thing to another to find out the חשׁבּון, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the balance of the account, and thus to reach a <hi type="italic">facit</hi>, a <hi type="italic">resultat</hi>.<note placement="foot">Cf. Aboth iv. 29, וגו ליתן, “to give account;” וגו הכל, “all according to the result.”</note> <div eID="gen12326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12327" type="x-p"/> That which presented itself to him in this way now follows. It was, in relation to woman, a negative experience: “What my soul sought on and on, and I found not, (is this).” The words are like the superscription of the following result, in which finally the זה of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.27">Ecc 7:27</reference></hi> terminates. Ginsburg, incorrectly: “what my soul is still seeking,” which would have required מבקּשׁת. The pret. בּקשׁה (with ק without <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.29">Ecc 7:29</reference>)<note placement="foot">As generally the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> forms of the root בקשׁ, Masor. all have <hi type="italic">Raphe</hi> on the ,ק except the imper. בּקּשׁוּ; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Luzzatto’s Gramm</hi>. §417.</note> is retrospective; and עוד, from עוּד, means <hi type="italic">redire</hi>, again and again, continually, as at Gen.. Gen 46:29. He always anew sought, and that, as biqshah naphshi for בקשׁתי denotes, with urgent striving, violent longing, and never found, viz., a woman such as she ought to be: a man, one of a thousand, I have found, etc. With right, the accentuation gives Garshayim to adam; it stands forth, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.20">Ecc 7:20</reference>, as a general denominator - the sequence of accents, <hi type="italic">Geresh</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pashta</hi>, <hi type="italic">Zakef</hi>, is as at Gen 1:9. “One among a thousand” reminds us of <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.3">Ecc 9:3</reference>; the old interpreters (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Dachselt’s <hi type="italic">Bibl. Accentuata</hi>), with reference to these parallels, connect with the one man among a thousand all kinds of incongruous christological thoughts. Only, here <hi type="italic">adam</hi>, like the Romanic <hi type="italic">l'homme</hi> and the like, means man in sexual contrast to woman. It is thus ideally meant, like ish, <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.9">1Sa 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.15">1Sa 6:15</reference>, and accordingly also the parall. אשּׁה. For it is not to be supposed that the author denies thereby perfect human nature to woman. But also Burger’s explanation: “a human being, whether man or woman,” is a useless evasion. Man has the name <hi type="italic">adam</hi> κατ ̓ ἐξ. by primitive hist. right: “for the man is not of the woman, but the woman of the man,” 1Co 11:8. The meaning, besides, is not that among a thousand human beings he found one upright man, but not a good woman (Hitz.), - for then the thousand ought to have had its proper denominator, אדם בני, - but that among a thousand persons of the male sex he found only one man such as he ought to be, and among a thousand of the female sex not one woman such as she ought to be; “among all these” is thus = among an equal number. Since he thus actually found the ideal of man only seldom, and that of woman still seldomer (for more than this is not denoted by the round numbers), the more surely does he resign himself to the following <hi type="italic">resultat</hi>, which he introduces by the word לבד (only, alone), as the clear gain of his searching:
entries.f15a5f8fa1a17c998b67a4c00fd5a3df4c85765e: <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.29">Ecc 7:29</reference> “Lo, this only have I found, that God created man upright; but they seek many arts.” Also here the order of the words is inverted, since זה, belonging as obj. to מץ (have I found), which is restricted by לבד, is amalgamated with ראה (Lo! see!). The author means to say: Only this (<hi type="italic">solummodo hocce</hi>) have I found, that ...; the ראה is an interjected <hi type="italic">nota bene</hi>. The expression: God has made man ישׁר, is dogmatically significant. Man, as he came from the Creator’s hand, was not placed in the state of moral decision, nor yet in the state of absolute indifference between good and evil; he was not neither good nor bad, but he was טוב, or, which is the same thing, ישׁר; <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, in every respect normal, so that he could normally develope himself from this positively good foundation. But by the expression ישׁר `שׁ, Koheleth has certainly not exclusively his origin in view, but at the same time his relative continuation in the propagation of himself, not without the concurrence of the Creator; also of man after the fall the words are true, ישׁר עשׂה, in so far as man still possesses the moral ability not to indulge sinful affections within him, nor suffer them to become sinful actions. But the sinful affections in the inborn nature of weak sinful man have derived so strong a support from his freedom, that the power of the will over against this power of nature is for the most part as weakness; the dominance of sin, where it is not counteracted by the grace of God, has always shown itself so powerful, that Koheleth has to complain of men of all times and in all circles of life: they seek many arts (as Luther well renders it), or properly, calculations, inventions, devices (hhishshevonoth,<note placement="foot">If we derive this word from hhěshbon, the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in the שׁ is the so-called <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi>.</note> as at <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.15">2Ch 26:15</reference>, from hhishshevon, which is as little distinguished from the formation hhěshbon, as hhizzayon from hhězyon), viz., of means and ways, by which they go astray from the normal natural development into abnormities. In other words: inventive refined degeneracy has come into the place of moral simplicity, ἁπλότης (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.3">2Ch 11:3</reference>). As to the opinion that caricatures of true human nature, contrasts between the actual and that which ought to be (the ideal), are common, particularly among the female sex, the author has testimonies in support of it from all nations. It is confirmed by the primitive history itself, in which the woman appears as the first that was led astray, and as the seducer (cf. <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. pp. 103-106). With reference to this an old proverb says: “Women carry in themselves a frivolous mind,” <hi type="italic">Kiddushin</hi> 80 <hi type="italic">b</hi>.<note placement="foot">Cf. Tendlau’s <hi type="italic">Sprichw</hi>. (1860), No. 733.</note> <div eID="gen12327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12328" type="x-p"/> And because a woman, when she has fallen into evil, surpasses a man in fiendish superiority therein, the Midrash reckons under this passage before us fifteen things of which the one is worse than the other; the thirteenth is death, and the fourteenth a bad woman.<note placement="foot">Duke’s <hi type="italic">Rabb. Blumenl</hi>. (1844), No. 32.</note> <div eID="gen12328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12329" type="x-p"/> Hitzig supposes that the author has before him as his model Agathoclea, the mistress of the fourth Ptolemy Philopator. But also the history of the Persian Court affords dreadful examples of the truth of the proverb: “Woe to the age whose leader is a woman;”<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Ibid</hi>. No. 118.</note> and generally the harem is a den of female wickedness.  <chapter eID="Eccl.7"/> <div eID="gen12329" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. VII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>Having largely discoursed of the vanity of all worldly things, and having now said in the foregoing verse, that no man knew what was best for him, he now proceeds to prescribe some Remedies against these Vanities, and to di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rect men to the right method of obtaining that felicity which is not to be ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pected or found in this World.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 A <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 15. 30. & 22. 1.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>Good</ns0:hi> name <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">A good and well-grounded report from wise and worthy per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> better than precious Oint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>A name,</ns0:hi> which is put for a good name by a Synec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doche, that only being worthy to be called a name, because evil and worthless men quickly lose their Name and Memory. Thus <ns0:hi>a Wife</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>a good Wife,</ns0:hi> Prov. 18. 22. and <ns0:hi>a day</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>a good day,</ns0:hi> Luk. 19. 41, 44.</ns0:note>: and the day of death <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To wit, of a good man, or one who hath left a good Name behind him, which is ea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sily understood both from the former clause, and from the nature of the thing; for to a wicked man this day is far worse, and most terrible. Yet if this passage be delivered with respect only to this Life, and abstracting from the future Life, as many other passages in this Book are to be understood, then this may be true in gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral of all men, and is the consequent of all the former discourse. Seeing this Life is so full of Vanity, and Vexation, and Misery, it is a more desirable thing for a man to go out of it, than to come into it. Which is the more considerable note, because it is contrary to the Opinion and Practice of almost all Mankind, to celebrate their own or Childrens Birth-days with solemn Feasts and rejoicings, and their deaths with all expressions of sorrow.</ns0:note>, than the day of ones birth. <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>b</ns0:hi> Which was very fragrant, and acceptable, and useful, and of great price, especially in those Countries. See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 24. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 92. 10. & 133. 2. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 39. 2.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> better to go to the house of mourning <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Where Mourners meet together to celebrate the Funerals of a deceased Friend.</ns0:note>, than to go to the house of feasting: for that <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To wit, death, the cause of that mourning.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the end of all men <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">It brings men to the serious consideration of their last end, which is their greatest Wisdom and Interest.</ns0:note>, and the living will lay <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> to his heart <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Will be seriously affected with it, and awakened to prepare for it; whereas feasting is com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly attended with Mirth, and Levity, and manifold Temptations, and indisposeth mens minds to Spiritual and Heavenly Thoughts. Hence it is evident that those passages of this Book which may seem to favour a sensual and voluptuous Life, are not spoken by <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> in his own Name, or as his Opinion, but in the person of an Epi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cure.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

They are constantly, or very frequently meditating upon sad and serious things, such as Death and Judgment, the Vanity of this Life, and the reality and eternity of the next; because they know that these thoughts, though they be not grateful to the sensual part, yet they are abso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lutely necessary, and highly profitable, and most comfortable in the end, which every wise man most regards.</ns0:note>; but the heart of fools <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the house of mirth <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Their minds and affections are wholly set upon feasting, and jolly, because, like Fools and brutish Creatures, they regard only their present delight, and mind not how dearly they must pay for them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> better to hear the rebuke of the wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which though it causeth some grief, yet frequently brings great benefit, even Reformation and Salvation, both from tempo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral and from eternal Destruction, both which are the portion of impenitent sinners.</ns0:note>, than for a man to hear the song <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The flatteries, or other merry discourses, which are as pleasant to corrupt Nature, as Songs or Musick.</ns0:note> of fools.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 For as the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a sound.</ns0:note> crackling of thorns <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which for a time make a great noise and blaze, but present<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly wast themselves, and go out without any considerable effect up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the meat in the pot.</ns0:note> under a pot, so <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">So vanishing and fruitless.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the laughter of the fool: this also <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> vanity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Surely oppression <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either 1 Active. When a wise Man falls into the practice of this sin of oppressing others, he is besotted by it, and by the vast Riches which he by his great wit gets by it. Or rather 2. Pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sive, when a wise man is oppressed by foolish and wicked men, it makes him fret and rage, and speak or act like a mad man; for the wisest men are most sensible of indignities and injuries, whereas fools are stupid, & do not much lay them to heart.</ns0:note> maketh a wise man mad, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 16. 19.</ns0:note> and a gift <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">A bribe given to a wise man.</ns0:note> destroyeth the heart <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Deprives him of the use of his understanding, which is oft called <ns0:hi>the heart,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 23. 8. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 16. 19. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 4. 18. or makes him mad, as was said in the former clause. So this verse discovers two ways whereby a wise man may be made mad by suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fering oppression from others, or by receiving bribes to oppress o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers. And this also is an argument of the vanity of worldly Wis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom, that it is so easily corrupted and lost, and so it serves the main design of this Book.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:551" />8 Better <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the end of a thing, than the beginning thereof <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">If this verse relates to that next foregoing, it is an Argument to keep mens minds from being disordered, either by oppression or bribery, because the end of those practices will shew, that he who oppresseth another, doth himself most hurt by it, and that he who taketh Bribes is no gainer by them.                   <ns0:p n="23">23 All this <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>All these things;</ns0:hi> of which I have here discoursed.</ns0:note> have I proved <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">I have diligently examined and found all this to be true.</ns0:note> by wisdom <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">By the help of that singular Wisdom which God had given me.</ns0:note>: I said, I will be wise <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">I de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />termined within my self that I would by all possible means seek to attain perfection of wisdom, and I persuaded my self that I should attain to it.</ns0:note>, but it <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> far from me <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">I found my self greatly disappointed, and the more I knew, the more I saw mine own folly and misery.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 28, 12, 20.</ns0:note> That which is far off, and exceeding deep, who can find it out <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">No human Wit can attain to perfect Wisdom, or to the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />act knowledg of Gods Counsels and Works, and the reasons of them, because they are unsearchably deep, and far above our <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ight, some of them being long since past, and therefore utterly unknown to us, and others yet to come which we cannot foreknow.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> I and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>art <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 17. & 2. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>2.</ns0:note> I applied mine heart <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I was not discouraged, but provoked by the difficulty of the work to undertake it: which is an argument of a great and generous Soul.</ns0:note> to know, and to search, and to seek out <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He useth three words signifying the same thing, to inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mate his vehement desire, and vigorous, and unwearied endeavor after it.</ns0:note> wisdom, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>the ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count,</ns0:hi> so Gr.</ns0:note> the reason <ns0:hi>of things</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Both of Gods various Providences, and of the differing and contrary counsels and courses of men.</ns0:note>, and to know the wickedness of folly <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">That I might clearly and fully understand the great evil of sin, and all that wickedness, and folly, or madness which is bound up in the hearts of all men by Nature, and which discovers it self in the course of their Lives.</ns0:note>, even of foolish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> madness.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Pro. 22. 14.</ns0:note> And I find <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">By my own sad Experience. Which <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> here records, partly as an instance of that folly and madness which he expressed in general, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 25. and partly as a testimony of his true Repentance, for his foul miscarriages, for which he was willing to take shame to himself, not only from the present, but from all succeeding genera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions.</ns0:note> more bitter <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">More vexatious and pernicious, as producing those hor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rours of Conscience, those reproaches, and diseases, and other plagues, both temporal and spiritual, from God, which are far worse than simple death, and, after all these, everlasting destruction.</ns0:note> than death, the wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The strange woman, of whom he speaks so much in the Proverbs.</ns0:note> whose heart <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> snares and nets <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Who being <ns0:hi>subtil of heart, Prov.</ns0:hi> 7. 10. is full of crafty devices to insnare men.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> her hands <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either by Gifts; or rather by lascivious Actions.</ns0:note> as bands <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Wherewith she holds them fast in cruel bondage, so that they have neither Power no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Will to forsake her, notwithstanding all the dangers and mischiefs which they know do attend upon such practices.</ns0:note>. <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. he that is <ns0:hi>good before God.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Whoso pleaseth God <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Heb. he that is <ns0:hi>good before God,</ns0:hi> either 1. Whom God loves and favours. Or rather 2. Who is good sincerely, or in the judgment of God who cannot be deceived; whereas Hypocrites are frequently good in the eyes or opinions of men. Which sense seems to be confirmed from the opposition of <ns0:hi>the sinner</ns0:hi> to him, both here, and <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 2. 26. Hereby he intimates that neither a good temper of mind, nor great discretion, nor good Education and In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction, nor any other thing, except Gods Grace, is a sufficient preservative from the dominion of this Lust.</ns0:note> shall escape from her <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Shall be prevent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from falling into that sin, or, if by surprisal or strong temptation he be drawn to it, he shall be recovered out of it by true Repentance.</ns0:note>, but the sinner <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The wilful and obstinate sinner, who gives himself up to the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon practice of this or other sins; he who is <ns0:hi>a sinner before the Lord,</ns0:hi> as the <ns0:hi>Sodomites</ns0:hi> are called, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 13. 13. who is fitly opposed to him that is <ns0:hi>good before God;</ns0:hi> he in whom there is not a dram of true goodness: for otherwise all men are sinners, as was said <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20.</ns0:note> shall be taken <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Shall be intangled and kept fast in her chains, as is implied, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause this is opposed to <ns0:hi>escaping from her.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> by her <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">It is a strange thing, and worthy of your serious observation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 Behold <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">It is a strange thing, and worthy of your serious observation.</ns0:note>, this have I found (saith the preacher <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>the penitent,</ns0:hi> who speaks what he hath learned, both by deep Study, and costly experience.</ns0:note>) <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, weigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:hi>one thing after <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> to find <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> the reason.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>counting</ns0:hi> one by one <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Considering things or persons very exactly and distinctly, one after another; and not only in ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neral and confusedly, in which case a man may very easily be mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />staken, and comparing them together, whereby I was enabled to make the truer judgment of them.</ns0:note>, to find out the account <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">That I might make a true and just estimate in this matter. Or, as it is in the margent, and was rendred <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 25. <ns0:hi>the reason,</ns0:hi> to wit, of that which I am about to say. I considered the persons severally and critically, that from thence I might understand the reason of the thing.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:552" />28 Which yet my soul seeketh <ns0:hi>y,</ns0:hi> but I find not <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">That it was so he <ns0:hi>found out,</ns0:hi> as he now said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27. but the whole truth and the reason of the thing he could not find out.</ns0:note>: one man <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">One worthy of the Name of a Man, a wise and vertuous Man. <ns0:hi>Man</ns0:hi> is put for a worthy or good Man, as <ns0:hi>Name</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>a good Name</ns0:hi> above <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. and <ns0:hi>Wise</ns0:hi> for a <ns0:hi>good Wife,</ns0:hi> as was noted before.</ns0:note> among a thousand <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">With whom I have conversed. He is supposed to mention this Number in allusion to his Thousand Wives and Concubines, as they are numbred by parcels, 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 11. 3.</ns0:note> have I found, but a wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">One worthy of that Name, one who is not a dishonour to her Kind and Sex, who is not brutish in her disposition and conversation.</ns0:note> among all those <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In that Thousand whom I have taken into intimate society with my self. Whereby he also passeth a severe censure upon himself that he had associated him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self with such Persons, and not with the vertuous Women, which doubtless there were in his time, as appears from <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 31. It is not <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s design to disparage this Sex, nor to make a general comparison between men and women in all Places, and Ages, but onely to suggest his own experience concerning it.</ns0:note> have I not found. <ns0:note place="bottom">It seemed so wonderful to me that I suspected I had not made a sufficient enquiry, & therefore I returned to search again with more earnestness and accuratness.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Lo, this onely have I found <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Though I could not find out all the streams of wickedness and their infinite windings and turnings in the World, yet I have disco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered the fountain of it, to wit, Original sin, and the corruption of Nature which is both in men and Women.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 1. 27.</ns0:note> that God hath made man <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">God made our first Parents, <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Eve.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> upright <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>right,</ns0:hi> without any imperfection or corruption, conformable to his Nature and Will, which is the rule of right, after his own likeness, understanding, and holy, and every way good.</ns0:note>; but they <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Our first Parents, and after them their Po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sterity treading in their steps.</ns0:note> have sought out many inventions <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Were not contented with their pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent state, but aimed at higher things, and studied new ways of making themselves more wise and happy, than God had made them, and readily hearkned to the suggestions of the Devil to that end. And we their sinful and wretched Children after their example are still prone to forsake the certain rule of God's Word, and the true way to happiness, and to seek new Methods and Inventions of attain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to it, even such as <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> hath discoursed of in this Book.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
